title: Weather, Climate and Atmospheric Histories

intro: Why do storms cross North America from west to east, and why do they spin opposite ways in the two hemispheres? Start with Earth's weather: heating, the Coriolis effect, clouds and the limits of forecasting. Then meet the four things that change a planet's climate and see, with real numbers, why light gases escape into space. Tour the airless Moon and Mercury, cold Mars that lost its air and water, and scorching Venus with its runaway greenhouse, then find out what keeps Earth's climate stable and what the evidence says about the warming people are causing today.

learningObjectives.text: What factors can cause long-term climate change?
How does a planet gain or lose atmospheric gases?
Do the Moon and Mercury have any atmosphere?
How has Mars's climate differed in the past?
How did Venus get so hot?
How did Earth's atmosphere end up so different?
Why does Earth's climate stay relatively stable?
What is the evidence for human-caused climate change?

sections.title: Weather versus climate

img.alt: A wiggly blue line of temperature over many years, labelled weather: the ever-changing mix of wind, clouds, temperature and pressure, with a flat red line through it labelled climate: the average of weather over many years. A note asks whether a few dry years are random weather or the start of a drier climate.

steps.title: Two time scales
bullets: **Weather** is the constantly changing mix of wind, clouds, temperature and pressure that makes one day hotter, cloudier or stormier than another.
**Climate** is the average of the weather over many years. A cold desert can still get the odd snowfall; its climate is still cold and dry.
Climates do change naturally, but usually slowly: over decades, centuries or thousands of years.
Over a human lifetime the two can be hard to separate. A drought of a few years might be random weather or the first sign of a drier climate.

steps.title: What drives weather
bullets: Wind, rain and the rest are all powered by **energy in the atmosphere**, so only a world with an atmosphere can have weather.
Earth has the most varied weather of the rocky planets, so it is the main example for how weather works.
Weather is so complex that local forecasts are reliable only about a week ahead, yet Earth as a whole shows clear, regular wind patterns.

boxes.text: Telling weather from climate matters most for judging whether people are changing the climate: one hot summer is weather, a decades-long trend is climate.
Weather is your mood today; climate is your personality.
Climate is NOT 'the weather in a place'; it is the AVERAGE of weather over many years (Book 10.2, p. 286). A single cold day says nothing about climate.

sections.title: Heating and circulation cells

img.alt: Animation: a globe lit by the Sun from the right with one large loop of air in each hemisphere. Dots ride the loops: warm air rises at the equator and flows toward the poles high up, then cool polar air sinks and returns to the equator along the surface. The loops are drawn much taller than the few kilometres they really are.

steps.title: Warm air rises at the equator
bullets: Two things shape global winds: **atmospheric heating** and **planetary rotation**.
The equator receives more solar heat than the poles. Warm equatorial air rises and flows toward the poles high up; cool polar air sinks and flows back toward the equator along the surface.
If rotation played no part, each hemisphere would have one giant loop of air, a **circulation cell** (also called a **Hadley cell**). The real cells reach only a few kilometres above the ground.

img.alt: Venus, Earth and Mars, each with an equator thermometer and a pole thermometer. On Venus both read hot because thick air carries heat to the poles; on Earth the pole is cooler but warmed by circulation; on Mars the thin air carries little heat and the pole is far colder than the equator.

steps.title: Cells carry heat poleward
bullets: Circulation cells move heat upward and from the equator toward the poles, so Earth's poles are much warmer than they would be without them.
**Venus**: the dense air carries so much heat that the equator and the poles are almost the same temperature.
**Mars**: the thin air carries very little heat, so the poles stay much colder than the equator.

boxes.text: Thicker air holds and carries more thermal energy, so the same circulation evens out temperatures far better on Venus than on Mars.
Hot air goes up and out to the poles; cold air comes down and back to the equator: a conveyor belt for heat.
Without rotation there would be ONE cell per hemisphere, not three (Book 10.2, p. 287, Figure 10.13); rotation is what splits Earth's cells.

sections.title: Rotation and the Coriolis effect

img.alt: Animation of a merry-go-round seen from above, turning counterclockwise. A red ball rolled inward from the edge and a blue ball rolled outward from near the centre both curve to the right of the dashed lines they were aimed along. Notes: the inward ball starts with the faster outer speed and gets ahead; the outward ball starts slow and lags; spinning the other way, both would veer left.

steps.title: The merry-go-round
bullets: On a spinning merry-go-round the outer edge moves faster than the middle, because it has farther to go each turn.
Roll a ball inward from the edge: it keeps its fast edge speed, gets ahead of the slower inner parts and veers to the **right** (for counterclockwise spin).
Roll it outward from near the centre: it starts slow, falls behind the faster outer parts and **also** veers right. On a clockwise merry-go-round both would veer left.
This sideways drift is the **Coriolis effect**.

img.alt: A globe with curved arrows. In the Northern Hemisphere, air moving north and air moving south both bend to their right; in the Southern Hemisphere they bend to their left. Notes explain that the equator circles the axis faster than the poles and that the effect matters only over hundreds of kilometres.

steps.title: On the rotating Earth
bullets: The equator circles Earth's axis faster than places near the poles.
Air moving away from the equator carries extra eastward speed and gets ahead of the ground; air moving toward the equator lags behind to the west.
Either way, moving air turns to its **right in the Northern Hemisphere** and to its **left in the Southern Hemisphere**.

img.alt: Animation of two storms, each around a low-pressure centre marked L. Arrows spiral inward. In the Northern Hemisphere the spiral turns counterclockwise; in the Southern Hemisphere it turns clockwise.

steps.title: Why storms spin
bullets: Uneven heating creates areas of slightly high (H) and low (L) pressure. Storms form around lows, which pull in air from all around.
The Coriolis effect turns the inflowing air, so storms swirl **counterclockwise in the north** and **clockwise in the south**.
This spin around a low can be very stable, so a storm can last days or weeks while it is carried across the globe.

img.alt: Left: a hurricane hundreds of kilometres across whose spin is set by the Coriolis effect. Right: a small sink drain under a metre across, where the Coriolis effect is far too weak; the bowl's shape and how the water started moving decide which way it swirls.

steps.title: The draining-sink myth
bullets: Hurricanes really do spin opposite ways in the two hemispheres, but sinks and toilets do not drain 'backward' south of the equator.

The Coriolis effect matters only when material moves much closer to or farther from the rotation axis, over **hundreds of kilometres**. For a drain it is negligible; the bowl's shape and how the water started moving decide.

boxes.text: Nothing pushes the air sideways: it keeps the speed it started with while the ground underneath moves at a different speed, so it drifts relative to the ground.
North: Right. South: Left. ('NR, SL' - Northern Right, Southern Left.)

Air bends right in the NORTHERN Hemisphere whether it moves north or south (Book 10.2, p. 287). Northern lows spin COUNTERclockwise even though the air turns right (Figure 10.15). The Coriolis effect does not decide how a toilet flushes (Common Misconceptions, p. 288).

sections.title: Three cells and Earth's wind belts

img.alt: A globe with three loops of circulating air in each hemisphere, split at about 30 and 60 degrees latitude. Labels: high latitudes 60-90 degrees, winds blow east to west; mid-latitudes 30-60 degrees, winds blow west to east; near the equator 0-30 degrees, winds blow east to west. The Coriolis effect turns north-south flow into east-west winds.

steps.title: Each big cell splits into three
bullets: Air flowing south from the North Pole along the ground would have to travel about 10,000 km to reach the equator. Long before then, the Coriolis effect turns it westward.
This splits each hemisphere's single cell into **three smaller cells** that turn like interlocking gears.

img.alt: Animation of a flat map striped by latitude with moving arrows: east-to-west winds near the equator and at high latitudes, west-to-east winds at mid-latitudes in both hemispheres. A storm cloud drifts eastward across the northern mid-latitudes, like storms crossing North America toward the east coast.

steps.title: The wind belts
bullets: In the cells nearest the equator and the poles, surface air flows toward the equator and is turned into winds that blow **east to west**.
In the mid-latitude cells, surface air flows toward the poles and is turned into winds that blow **west to east**.
That is why storms usually hit the west coast of the United States first and then move east across the continent.
In short, rotation turns north-south flow into east-west winds.

img.alt: Venus, Earth, Mars and a striped Jupiter side by side. Venus spins very slowly, so its Coriolis effect is very weak and it has two big cells; Earth's is strong enough to split each cell into three; small Mars has a weak effect; huge, fast Jupiter has many smaller cells.

steps.title: Coriolis on other planets
bullets: The Coriolis effect works on every planet. **Larger size** and **faster rotation** both make it stronger.
Only Earth, among the rocky planets, has a Coriolis effect strong enough to split its two big cells.

**Venus** has a very weak effect because it spins so slowly; **Mars** has a weak one because it is small. Huge, fast-spinning **Jupiter** and the other jovian planets have their cells split into many.

boxes.text: The mid-latitude cell is turned by its neighbours like a middle gear, so its surface air runs poleward, the opposite way to the other two cells, and the Coriolis effect turns it eastward.
Equator and poles: 'Easterlies' at both ends. The middle is the odd one out: west to east.

Mid-latitude winds blow FROM west TO east; equatorial and high-latitude winds blow east to west (Book 10.2, Figure 10.12). Mars's weak Coriolis effect comes from its small size, Venus's from its slow spin (p. 289).

sections.title: Clouds, rain and forecasts

img.alt: Animation: vapour rises from the ocean, a cloud forms high above a mountain, and drops grow and fall as rain on the land. Labels: 1, water evaporates; 2, convection carries the vapour up to cooler air; 3, it condenses into droplets or ice flakes, a cloud; 4, drops grow larger; 5, too heavy to stay up, they fall as rain, snow or hail.

steps.title: From vapour to rain
bullets: Rain, snow and hail together are **precipitation**, and precipitation needs clouds.
Clouds are tiny droplets of liquid water or flakes of ice, made when **water vapour condenses**.

The cycle: water evaporates from the surface; **convection** lifts the vapour to high, cold parts of the troposphere; it condenses into a cloud; the drops or flakes grow; when updrafts can no longer hold them up they fall as rain, snow or hail.
Wind forced up over mountains can also lift air high enough to make clouds.

img.alt: Sunlight bouncing off the top of a cloud back to space, and infrared arrows from the ground going up into the cloud and back down. Labels: cooling, clouds reflect sunlight; warming, clouds are made of greenhouse molecules that hold in infrared heat.

steps.title: Clouds cool and warm
bullets: Clouds are made from minor ingredients of the air, yet they have big effects.
They **reflect sunlight** back to space, which cools the surface, but they are also made of **greenhouse molecules**, which warm it.

img.alt: A green globe with a dark green rainy band at the equator and sandy bands at about 25 degrees north and south. Notes: the equator gets the most sunlight and convection, so lots of rain and jungles; the cells carry the dried-out air away and it sinks at 20-30 degrees, making deserts; summer afternoon convection brings thunderstorms.

steps.title: Jungles and deserts
bullets: Stronger convection means more clouds and rain. That is why thunderstorms are common on summer afternoons, when the sun-warmed ground drives strong convection.
The equator gets the most sunlight, the most convection and the most rain: lush jungles.
The rain wrings the moisture out of the air, and the circulation cells carry that dried air away from the equator, leaving little rain for latitudes of **20-30° north or south**: deserts.

img.alt: Animation of a graph over 30 days with two forecast lines, blue and red, that start almost the same, stay together for the first few days and then wander completely apart by a month. A grey band marks the long-term average, which stays predictable: climate models remain reliable even when weather cannot be forecast.

steps.title: Why forecasts fail after about a week
bullets: A forecast needs the current state of the weather (the **initial conditions**) and the physical laws for how it changes. Scientists run a computer 'model world' with both.

Change the starting wind speed slightly over Brazil and tomorrow's New York forecast barely changes, but next month's may be completely different. This extreme sensitivity is the **butterfly effect**, the hallmark of a **chaotic system** described by nonlinear equations.

Chaotic does not mean random: weather is 'predictably unpredictable'. Because **climate** is the long-term average, the chaos averages out, so climate models can be trusted far beyond the week or so that weather forecasts last.

boxes.text: Rising air cools; cool air holds less vapour, so it condenses. Anything that lifts air (convection or mountains) makes clouds.
Evaporate, Elevate, Condense, Grow, Fall.

Unpredictable weather does NOT make climate predictions unreliable: climate is an average, so the chaos averages out (Book 10.2, Special Topic, p. 289). Deserts at 20-30° are caused by dry air from the circulation cells, not by distance from the Sun (p. 290).

sections.title: Four causes of long-term climate change

img.alt: Four cards: 1, solar brightening, slow and noticeable only over tens of millions of years; 2, changes in axis tilt, which make seasons more or less extreme; 3, changes in reflectivity from ice, clouds or volcanic dust; 4, changes in greenhouse gases, more warms and less cools.

steps.title: The four factors
bullets: Scientists recognize four major causes of long-term climate change on rocky worlds: **solar brightening**, **changes in axis tilt**, **changes in reflectivity** and **changes in greenhouse gas abundance**.
More than one can act at the same time.

img.alt: A small young Sun labelled dimmer and a larger Sun today labelled about 30% brighter, joined by an arrow spanning about 4 billion years. A note says the change is too slow to notice over less than tens of millions of years and other factors can outweigh it.

steps.title: Solar brightening
bullets: Models of the Sun and observations of Sun-like stars show the Sun brightens with age: it is probably about **30% brighter** now than when the solar system was young.
The effect is noticeable only over **tens of millions of years** or more, and other factors can easily overwhelm it.
Proof: brightening alone would make every planet warmer now than in the past, yet Mars and Earth were both warmer at times early on.

img.alt: Animation: Earth's tilted axis rocks slowly back and forth while a label counts between 22 and 25 degrees (today about 23.5). Cards: more tilt brings hotter summers and colder winters and less ice, so warmer overall; less tilt lets ice build up, cooler, matching past ice ages; these Milankovitch cycles come from small gravity tugs.

steps.title: Changes in axis tilt
bullets: Small gravitational tugs from moons, other planets and the Sun can change a planet's tilt over thousands to millions of years. Earth's tilt is about **23.5°** now and has ranged from about **22° to 25°**.
**More tilt**: more extreme seasons. Warmer summers stop ice building up, so the planet reflects less and warms overall.
**Less tilt**: milder seasons; ice can build up and the planet cools. Times of smaller tilt match Earth's ice ages over the past few million years.
These cyclic changes in tilt and orbit are called **Milankovitch cycles**. Mars probably has far larger swings.

img.alt: Four cards. Reflect more and cool: ice and snow, more clouds, volcanic dust. Reflect less and warm: open water where sea ice was, shrinking ice caps. People raise reflectivity with smog and by cutting forests. People lower it with roads and cities and by melting Arctic sea ice.

steps.title: Changes in reflectivity
bullets: A planet that reflects more sunlight absorbs less and cools.

Volcanic eruptions release tiny dust particles called **aerosols** that reflect sunlight; cooling can last years if they reach the stratosphere. Growing ice caps and more clouds also raise reflectivity (though clouds add greenhouse warming too).

People change reflectivity both ways: smog and deforestation raise it, while roads, cities and the loss of Arctic sea ice lower it (water reflects much less sunlight than ice). The net direction and size are not yet certain.

img.alt: Two rows of linked boxes. Top, in red: more greenhouse gas, the planet warms, more water vaporizes into the air, air pressure rises. Bottom, in blue: less greenhouse gas, the planet cools, some gases freeze out, air pressure may drop.

steps.title: Changes in greenhouse gases
bullets: Probably the **most important** factor: more greenhouse gas strengthens the greenhouse effect and the planet warms; less weakens it and the planet cools.
Enough warming can vaporize more water, adding gas and raising the air pressure. Enough cooling can freeze gases out, lowering the pressure.
Changes in greenhouse gases seem to have had the biggest effect on the long-term climates of Venus, Earth and Mars.

boxes.text: Every factor works by changing the planet's energy balance: how much sunlight arrives, how much is absorbed, or how easily infrared heat escapes.
S-T-R-G: Sun, Tilt, Reflectivity, Greenhouse.

Greater tilt makes the planet WARMER overall (less ice), not colder (Book 10.2, p. 291). Solar brightening is far too slow to explain changes over centuries (p. 290). Deforestation INCREASES reflectivity; cities DECREASE it (p. 291).

sections.title: How atmospheres gain and lose gas

img.alt: Three ways to gain gas over the ground: a volcano puffing gas (outgassing of water, carbon dioxide, nitrogen and sulfur gases, the main source), a pool and a patch of ice giving off vapour (vaporization), and small particles striking bare ground and knocking atoms up (surface ejection, only on worlds with almost no air).

steps.title: Three sources of gas
bullets: **Outgassing** by volcanoes was the main source of air for Venus, Earth and Mars. Ice-rich planetesimals from beyond the frost line brought water and gas that were trapped inside the planets as they formed. Volcanoes mostly release water vapour, carbon dioxide, nitrogen and sulfur gases.
**Vaporization**: gases that condensed into surface liquids or ices can later evaporate or sublimate, a secondary source that grows when a planet warms.

**Surface ejection**: micrometeorites, solar wind particles and high-energy photons knock atoms off the ground. This only matters on worlds with almost no air, because a real atmosphere stops these particles before they reach the ground.

img.alt: Four cards in two columns. Can be undone: condensation, gas falling back as rain, snow or frost such as dry ice on Mars; chemical reactions, gas locked into rock or metal like rust. Permanent: thermal escape, fast particles reaching escape velocity; solar wind stripping where there is no magnetosphere.

steps.title: Four ways to lose gas
bullets: **Condensation** (gas falls as rain, snow or frost; carbon dioxide freezes into dry ice on Mars) and **chemical reactions** (gas locked into rock or metal, as when iron rusts) only move gas to the surface or interior. They can be reversed.

**Thermal escape** (a particle in the exosphere reaches escape velocity) and **solar wind stripping** (solar wind particles sweep gas away from a world with no protective magnetosphere) remove gas **permanently**.

img.alt: Three cards: small worlds have low escape velocity; worlds near the Sun have hotter, faster gas; light gases such as hydrogen and helium escape far more easily than carbon dioxide, nitrogen or oxygen. Below: the rocky planets lost their hydrogen and helium but Venus, Earth and Mars kept heavier gases from volcanoes.

steps.title: Who loses gas most easily?
bullets: Thermal escape is strongest on **small** worlds (low escape velocity), worlds **close to the Sun** (hotter, faster gas) and for **light gases** such as hydrogen and helium.

All the rocky planets are small and warm enough to lose hydrogen and helium, so none kept those gases from the solar nebula. Venus, Earth and Mars held on to the heavier gases released later by outgassing.

boxes.text: Gas that condenses or reacts is still on the planet and can come back; gas that escapes to space is gone.
Gain: Out-Vap-Eject. Lose: two that 'park' gas (condense, react) and two that 'launch' it (escape, strip).

Surface ejection is NOT a source for planets that already have thick air (Book 10.2, p. 292). Condensation and chemical reactions are reversible; only thermal escape and solar wind stripping are permanent (Figure 10.21). Only water existed in modest amounts in the solar nebula; the other outgassed gases formed by chemistry inside the planets (p. 291 footnote).

sections.title: Thermal escape by the numbers

img.alt: Graph of how many sodium atoms in the Moon's 400 K exosphere move at each speed: a hump peaking near 0.5 km/s (the peak thermal velocity) with a thin shaded tail beyond the escape velocity line at 2.4 km/s. Beside it, an animation of atoms bouncing above the ground while a few fast red ones fly off the top for good.

steps.title: Many speeds at once
bullets: Gas particles keep colliding, so at any moment they move at a wide range of speeds. The spread has a typical shape that depends on the temperature and the particle mass.
The most common speed, the peak of the curve, is the **peak thermal velocity**.

A particle can escape only if it reaches **escape velocity**, is moving upward and does not hit anything on the way out. Even when the peak is well below escape velocity, a small fast fraction always can, and collisions keep refilling that fast tail.

img.alt: The formula v thermal equals the square root of 2kT over m, where T is temperature in kelvin, m the mass of one particle and k is 1.38 x 10^-23 joule per kelvin. Cards: four times the temperature doubles the speed; four times the mass halves it. Rule of thumb: a gas faster than about 20% of escape velocity is lost within a few billion years.

steps.title: The formula
bullets: **v_thermal = √(2kT / m)**, where T is the temperature in kelvin, m the mass of one particle and k = 1.38 x 10^-23 joule/K (Boltzmann's constant).
Hotter gas moves faster: **four times the temperature doubles the speed**. Heavier particles move slower: **four times the mass halves it**.
Rule of thumb: if a gas's peak thermal velocity is more than about **20% of the escape velocity**, it will be completely lost within a few billion years, less than the age of the solar system.

img.alt: Bar chart of peak thermal speeds on the Moon at 400 K against its escape velocity of 2.4 km/s: hydrogen 2.6 km/s, past the line, so it escapes quickly; sodium 0.5 km/s, about 20% of escape, so it leaks slowly and is topped up from the surface.

steps.title: Worked example: the Moon
bullets: The Moon's daytime temperature is 400 K and its escape velocity is about 2.4 km/s.
Hydrogen atoms (1.67 x 10^-27 kg): v = √(2 x 1.38 x 10^-23 x 400 / 1.67 x 10^-27) ≈ 2,600 m/s = **2.6 km/s**, a little above escape velocity, so hydrogen escapes quickly.

Sodium atoms are about 23 times heavier and peak near **0.5 km/s**, only about 20% of escape velocity. They leak away slowly and are continually replaced from the surface, so the Moon has a thin **sodium exosphere**.

boxes.text: Temperature sets the average kinetic energy per particle. At the same energy, a lighter particle must move faster.
Speed goes with the square root: x4 temperature gives x2 speed; x4 mass gives half the speed; x9 gives x3 or a third.

Thermal escape does NOT need the typical particle to reach escape velocity: the fast tail leaks away anyway (Book, Mathematical Insight 10.2, p. 293). Doubling the temperature does not double the speed; it multiplies it by √2 (about 1.4).

sections.title: The Moon and Mercury: almost airless

img.alt: A grey lunar landscape under a black sky with the bright Sun, labelled: black sky even in daylight, too little gas to scatter light. Cards: no absorption so no troposphere, stratosphere or thermosphere, only an exosphere; frozen, the whole atmosphere would almost fit in a dorm room; rare collisions let particles reach thousands of kilometres up.

steps.title: Only an exosphere
bullets: The Moon and Mercury are not completely without gas, but it is far too thin to scatter or absorb sunlight.
No scattering: even at noon you would see a **pitch-black sky** around the bright Sun.
No absorption: there is no troposphere, stratosphere or thermosphere, only an extremely thin **exosphere**.

Frozen solid, either world's whole atmosphere would almost fit in a dorm room. Collisions are so rare that particles rise as high as their speed allows, so these exospheres reach thousands of kilometres up.

img.alt: Animation: micrometeorites, solar wind particles and solar photons hit the bare grey ground and knock atoms loose. Most atoms fly in arcs hundreds of kilometres long and land again, bouncing a few dozen times before being absorbed; a red atom fast enough to escape keeps going up.

steps.title: Where their gas comes from
bullets: Any gas from ancient volcanoes is long gone, lost to thermal escape (and some probably to the solar wind). Neither world has active volcanoes now.
Mercury loses gas because it is small and hot in the day; the Moon is cooler but smaller, with a lower escape velocity, so gas escapes about as easily from both.

The only ongoing source is **surface ejection** by micrometeorites, solar wind particles and solar photons. The gas never builds up: some atoms escape at once, the rest bounce in arcs hundreds of kilometres long, a few dozen times, until the surface absorbs them.

img.alt: A cross-section of a deep crater near a pole with the Sun low on the horizon: sunlight skims over the rim and never reaches the floor, where a layer of water ice sits in permanent shadow. Notes: the ice probably came from comet impacts; there is no liquid water because there is almost no air pressure.

steps.title: Ice in polar craters
bullets: With almost no air pressure, liquid water cannot exist on either world, and sunlit ice would long ago have vaporized and escaped.

Yet spacecraft have confirmed an old prediction: both have **water ice at the bottoms of craters near their poles**, where the floors are in permanent shadow. The ice probably came from comet impacts and built up over millions of years.

The Moon also seems to have small amounts of water chemically bound in its upper soil over much of its surface; its origin is unknown. None of this water trades with the atmosphere today, but lunar water could be very useful to future colonists.

boxes.text: Light is scattered and absorbed only when there is enough gas in its path. With so few atoms, sunlight passes straight through to the ground.
Moon and Mercury: 'all exosphere, no layers, no sky colour'.

The Moon and Mercury DO have an atmosphere, just an extremely thin exosphere (Book 10.3, p. 292). Its gas comes from surface ejection, not volcanoes (p. 293). The Moon, though cooler, loses gas about as easily as Mercury because it is smaller (p. 293).

sections.title: Mars today

img.alt: A red Mars with a white polar cap and four cards: air pressure under 1% of Earth's, so liquid water is unstable; mostly carbon dioxide but too little gas for a strong greenhouse; average about -50 degrees C; no ozone layer, so harsh ultraviolet reaches the ground.

steps.title: A thin, cold desert
bullets: Mars's surface looks like an Earth desert or volcanic plain, but its air is very different.
Pressure is **under 1% of Earth's**, so liquid water is unstable on the surface and astronauts would need pressurized suits.
The air is mostly carbon dioxide, but there is so little of it that the greenhouse effect is weak. The average temperature is about **-50°C**.
With little oxygen there is **no ozone layer**, so much of the Sun's harmful ultraviolet reaches the ground.

img.alt: Mars's stretched orbit around an off-centre Sun. On the near side Mars is closer and moving fast: southern summer is short and warm while northern winter is short and mild. On the far side it is farther and slower: southern winter is long and frigid, northern summer long and cool.

steps.title: Uneven seasons
bullets: Mars's axis tilt is similar to Earth's, so it has seasons. But its **more elliptical orbit** also matters.

Mars is much closer to the Sun during southern summer, so the **southern hemisphere has more extreme seasons**: short, warm summers and long, cold winters. The north has a long cool summer and a short mild winter.

img.alt: Animation of Mars through a year: the polar cap at the winter pole grows with frozen carbon dioxide while the summer cap shrinks to its water-ice core, and white arrows show wind blowing from the summer pole toward the winter pole. Notes: the winter pole reaches about -130 degrees C, and up to a third of the atmosphere moves pole to pole.

steps.title: Carbon dioxide swaps poles
bullets: At the winter pole the temperature drops to about **-130°C**, cold enough for carbon dioxide to freeze into dry ice on the polar cap.
At the summer pole the dry ice vaporizes; by midsummer only a leftover cap of **water ice** remains.
The pressure rises at the summer pole and falls at the winter pole. Up to **a third** of the whole atmosphere moves between the poles each year.

img.alt: A dusty yellow-brown Martian sky over red ground with a tall swirling dust devil rising from the ground. Notes: dust devils are air heated from below, some 800 m or more tall; seasonal winds raise dust storms that can hide almost the whole planet; settling dust once fooled astronomers into seeing seasonal plants; without dust the sky would be nearly black.

steps.title: Wind and dust
bullets: The strong winds from this seasonal flow can start huge **dust storms**, especially as the more extreme southern summer approaches. At times dust hides almost the whole surface.
Settling dust can change how large areas look, which once fooled astronomers into thinking they saw plants changing with the seasons.
**Dust devils**, swirls of air heated from below by the sunlit ground, are common in summer and can be much larger than on Earth (one reached at least 800 m).
The air is so thin that without dust the sky would be nearly black; dust scatters light and gives it a **yellow-brown** colour.

img.alt: Two cross-sections. A polar cap: a thin layer of carbon dioxide ice a few metres thick on top of a thick body of water ice. Buried ice: glaciers and dusty ice layers under a cover of rocks and dust, found by radar, with an icy cliff at 57 degrees south. Banner: melted, the known ice would cover Mars at least 20 to 30 metres deep.

steps.title: Water locked as ice
bullets: There is no liquid water on the surface today, but there is a lot of **water ice**.

The polar caps are mostly water ice under a thin layer (a few metres at most) of carbon dioxide ice. Radar has found vast dusty ice layers around both poles and glaciers at lower latitudes, protected by rock and dust. A cliff at 57°S exposes ice reaching within a metre or two of the surface.
Melted, all the known ice would cover Mars to an average depth of at least about **20 to 30 metres**.

boxes.text: The air is too thin for a strong greenhouse or for liquid water: low pressure makes water boil or freeze instead of staying liquid.
Mars's weather is 'CO2 commuting' from pole to pole with the seasons.

Mars's south has the MORE extreme seasons because of its elliptical orbit, not its tilt (Book 10.4, p. 295). The leftover summer cap is WATER ice; the seasonal frost is CO2 (p. 295, Figure 10.25). Dust devils rise from the ground; they do not come down from the sky like tornadoes (p. 295).

sections.title: How Mars's climate has changed

img.alt: Animation: Mars's axis swings slowly from upright to tipped far over while a label counts from 0 to 60 degrees. Cards: a small tilt freezes CO2 at the poles, thinning the air and cooling Mars; a large tilt warms the summer pole and thickens the air; the swings are big because Jupiter tugs harder and the tiny moons cannot steady the axis.

steps.title: Tilt-driven climate cycles
bullets: Mars's climate changes little from year to year, but calculations suggest its tilt swings from about **0° to about 60°** over hundreds of thousands to millions of years.

Two reasons: **Jupiter** tugs harder on Mars's axis because Mars orbits closer to it, and Mars's tiny moons, **Phobos and Deimos**, are too small to steady its axis the way our large Moon steadies Earth's.
**Small tilt**: the poles stay frozen for tens of thousands of years; more CO2 freezes out, the air thins, the greenhouse weakens and the whole planet cools.

**Large tilt**: the summer pole warms, water ice and CO2 vaporize, the air thickens and Mars warms, though probably not enough for stable liquid water. Layers of dust and ice at the poles record these cycles.

img.alt: Three bars showing how deep Mars's water would be as a global layer: ice known today, at least about 20-30 m; from the deuterium-to-hydrogen ratio, more than 50 m; from some geology studies, close to 500 m. A note says volcanoes should have made the air about 400 times denser than today.

steps.title: Once warmer and wetter
bullets: Geological evidence shows water flowed and rain fell on Mars, but only **before about 3 billion years ago**. That needs warmth and enough pressure, so early Mars must have had a much **thicker atmosphere and stronger greenhouse**.
Volcanoes should have outgassed enough CO2 to make the air about **400 times as dense** as today, and enough water for oceans tens or hundreds of metres deep.
The ratio of deuterium to hydrogen in the air suggests enough water to cover Mars **more than 50 m** deep (one reason some suspect a northern ocean); some geology studies suggest close to **500 m**.

steps.title: An open debate
bullets: Models say that if today's Mars had its expected ancient CO2 and water, it would be warm enough, with enough pressure, for liquid water.

But the young Sun was dimmer, so even more greenhouse warming was needed, and its source is a mystery. Carbon dioxide ice clouds or methane might have kept Mars warm and wet for a billion years or more.
Others doubt the greenhouse was ever that strong; then Mars may have had only short rainy spells, perhaps triggered by large impacts, with lakes and oceans ice-covered for long periods.

boxes.text: Liquid water needs both warmth and pressure. Signs of rain mean the ancient air was much thicker than today's.
Mars has two clocks: a short tilt clock (up to millions of years) and one long one-way change (billions of years) from warm and wet to cold and dry.

Mars's tilt swings MORE than Earth's because of Jupiter and its tiny moons, not because it spins faster (Book 10.4, p. 296). Even a large tilt probably does not make liquid water stable (p. 297). The rainy period ended about 3 billion years ago (p. 297).

sections.title: Why Mars changed

img.alt: Two panels. Early Mars: a hot glowing core, a thick blue halo of air, lots of volcanism, a magnetic field shielding the air, a strong greenhouse with rain and rivers. Mars today: a cooled core, a thin halo, little volcanism, no global magnetic field so the solar wind strips the air, a weak greenhouse.

steps.title: Interior cooling and a lost shield
bullets: Mars must have lost most of the CO2 that once filled its air, weakening the greenhouse until the planet froze.
The leading idea links this to its **magnetic field**. Early on, convecting molten metal in its core and its rotation should have made a magnetic field and a protective magnetosphere.
As the small planet cooled, core convection stopped and the field weakened. Sunlight or chemistry split CO2 molecules into carbon and oxygen atoms, and the **solar wind stripped** them away.

img.alt: Mars with arrows of gas leaving into space toward the solar wind from the Sun. Labels: most of the carbon dioxide was lost to space, split into carbon and oxygen atoms and swept off by the solar wind once the magnetic field faded; some froze into the polar caps; some is locked into carbonate rocks.

steps.title: Where the carbon dioxide went
bullets: Some CO2 condensed into the **polar caps**; orbiters and rovers show some is locked in **carbonate rocks**. But the **bulk was probably lost to space**.

NASA's **MAVEN** orbiter (at Mars since 2014) measures carbon and oxygen atoms escaping today. Working back from the present loss rate confirms Mars once had far more CO2. The EscaPADE mission's two orbiters will build on these results.

img.alt: Animation: a wavy ultraviolet ray hits a water molecule; the two hydrogen atoms fly off upward and the oxygen sinks toward the red rocky ground. Labels: 1, with no ozone layer, ultraviolet splits water; 2, light hydrogen escapes to space so the water cannot re-form; 3, the oxygen goes too, some to the solar wind and the rest into rusting rock. Loss speeds up in southern summer.

steps.title: Where the water went
bullets: Some water is frozen in the caps and underground and some may be bound in crustal rocks, but most is probably **gone for good**, lost in a different way from the CO2.

Without an ultraviolet-absorbing stratosphere, **UV photons split water molecules**; the light **hydrogen** then escaped by **thermal escape**, so the water could never re-form. MAVEN sees this hydrogen loss, faster in southern summer when warmth and dust storms lift water higher.
The leftover oxygen went too: some to the solar wind, the rest into **chemical reactions with surface rock**, literally rusting Mars and giving the red planet its colour.

steps.title: Saltier, more acidic water
bullets: Older sediments seem to have formed in purer water than younger ones.

A simple explanation: volcanoes released sulfur gases that dissolved in the water, making it more acidic so it could dissolve more salts. Over time Martian water became saltier and more acidic. Rover studies agree: low-lying rocks explored by Curiosity formed in purer water than rocks higher up or at the Opportunity site.

steps.title: Size was the critical factor
bullets: Mars was big enough for volcanoes to release water and gas early on, but **too small to keep the internal heat** needed to hold them.

As it cooled, outgassing slowed, while weak gravity and the lost magnetic field let gas be stripped away. An Earth-sized Mars might have a moderate climate today; a Mars closer to the Sun might still have flowing water.
A world with streams, rain, lakes and perhaps oceans became a frozen desert at least 3 billion years ago, a warning of how drastically a climate can change.

boxes.text: Small planets cool fast: a cold core stops the magnetic dynamo and the volcanoes, so the shield goes and the supply of new gas dries up together.
Mars lost its CO2 to the WIND (solar wind stripping) and its water to the SUN (UV splitting, then hydrogen escape).

Mars's CO2 went mostly to SPACE, not into the polar caps (Book 10.4, p. 297). Water was lost mainly by UV splitting and hydrogen escape, not by the solar wind (p. 299). Releasing the polar-cap CO2 ('terraforming') could not restore the old atmosphere, because most of it is gone (Think About It, p. 299).

sections.title: Venus today

img.alt: A dim orange view of Venus's surface: overcast reddish-orange sky over dark ground, about 470 degrees C day and night. Cards: pressure 90 times Earth's, like nearly 1 km under the ocean; hotter than a self-cleaning oven; almost all carbon dioxide with no oxygen; air about 10% as dense as water.

steps.title: On the surface
bullets: Venus kept more interior heat than Mars because it is larger, so it had more volcanism, and outgassing released the huge amount of CO2 behind its strong greenhouse effect.
On the surface: heat beyond a self-cleaning oven and pressure **90 times Earth's**, like being nearly 1 km under the ocean.
The air is almost all **carbon dioxide** with virtually no oxygen, so it is unbreathable even if cooled.

The air is about **10% as dense as water**: moving through it would be like swimming and flying at once. The thick air scatters away nearly all blue light, so the dim overcast sky looks **reddish-orange**.

img.alt: Two bands. High up, about 400 degrees C cooler than the ground: sulfuric acid clouds, acid rain that evaporates at least 30 km above the surface, winds that circle the planet in 4 days. At the surface: slow 243-day rotation, weak Coriolis effect, winds of a few km/h, no storms or rain. Cards: two big cells, same temperature everywhere, no seasons.

steps.title: Dull weather below, lively above
bullets: Venus spins slowly (243 Earth days), so its **Coriolis effect is very weak**: little surface wind (the Venera landers measured at most about 6 km/h) and never any hurricane-like storms. Venus has just **two large circulation cells**.
No rain reaches the ground: drops falling from the cool upper air evaporate first.

The thick air moves heat so well that the temperature is the same everywhere: poles as hot as the equator, night as hot as day. Virtually **no axis tilt** means no seasons (its listed tilt of 177.3° is nearly 180°, the same as 0° upside down, because Venus spins backward).

Higher up, where it is about 400°C cooler, **sulfuric acid** condenses into the bright clouds; acid rain evaporates at least 30 km above the surface. High winds circle the planet in just **4 days**, much faster than it rotates; no one knows why.

boxes.text: Slow spin means a weak Coriolis effect, so there is nothing to split the cells or spin up storms; thick air means heat is spread evenly.
Venus surface forecast: 'hot, heavy, still and dry, every day, everywhere'.

Venus's surface winds are WEAK; the fast 4-day winds are high in the clouds (Book 10.5, p. 300). Venus's tilt of 177° means essentially NO tilt, not a huge one (p. 300 footnote). The rain is sulfuric acid and never reaches the ground (p. 300).

sections.title: Where Venus's water and CO2 went

img.alt: Two bar pairs. Venus: a tall bar of carbon dioxide in the air (nearly 200,000 times Earth's air) and almost none in rock, because it has no oceans. Earth: almost none in the air and a tall bar locked in carbonate rocks such as limestone. Title: about the same total carbon dioxide, stored in different places.

steps.title: Same gases, different storage
bullets: Distance alone does not explain Venus's heat: its bright clouds reflect so much sunlight that without a greenhouse effect Venus would be quite cold.
The real cause is the huge amount of CO2 in its air, nearly **200,000 times** as much as in Earth's.

Venus and Earth are similar in size and make-up, so both should have outgassed similar amounts of water and CO2. Earth's water rained into oceans; its CO2 dissolved in water and formed **carbonate rocks** such as limestone.
Earth has about 200,000 times as much CO2 locked in rocks as in its air, so it has almost as much total CO2 as Venus. If it were in our air, Earth would be nearly as hot as Venus.

img.alt: Two boxes of hydrogen atoms (small white dots) with a few heavier deuterium atoms (larger purple dots). At the start there are many hydrogen atoms; after ultraviolet splits water and most hydrogen escapes, few hydrogen atoms remain but the deuterium is still there. Note: deuterium makes up about 100 times more of the hydrogen on Venus than on Earth.

steps.title: The missing water
bullets: Venus is incredibly dry: too hot for liquid water, ice or even water bound in surface rock, with very little in its air. Its total water is about **100,000 times less** than Earth's.
That is why its CO2 stays in the air: without oceans, CO2 cannot dissolve or be locked away in carbonate rock.

Leading idea: solar **ultraviolet split** the water molecules, the **hydrogen escaped** by thermal escape, and the oxygen was lost to reactions with rock and to **solar wind stripping** (Venus has no magnetic field to protect it).

Evidence: **deuterium**, hydrogen with an extra neutron (about 1 in 6,400 hydrogen atoms in Earth's oceans), is twice as heavy and escapes less easily. On Venus the fraction of deuterium is **about 100 times higher** than on Earth, so a lot of hydrogen from water has been lost to space.

boxes.text: Oceans are the key: they rain the water out of the air (protecting it from UV) and pull CO2 into rock. No oceans means water is destroyed and CO2 piles up.
Earth hid its CO2 in rock; Venus kept its CO2 in the sky.

Venus would be COLD without its greenhouse effect, because its clouds reflect so much sunlight (Book 10.5, p. 300). Earth has nearly as much CO2 as Venus, mostly in carbonate rocks (p. 301). Heavy water behaves chemically like ordinary water; the deuterium stays behind only because it is heavier and escapes less easily (p. 301).

sections.title: The runaway greenhouse effect

img.alt: Two loops. Self-reinforcing (positive) feedback: speaker sound, microphone picks it up, louder from the speaker, round and round into a screech. Self-regulating (negative) feedback: the screech makes the person move the microphone away and the sound calms. Note: runaway warming is self-reinforcing; Earth's CO2 cycle is self-regulating.

steps.title: Feedback
bullets: A **feedback process** is one where a change amplifies or counteracts itself.
**Self-reinforcing (positive) feedback** amplifies itself, like a microphone held too close to a speaker that ends in a screech.
**Self-regulating (negative) feedback** pushes back, like the embarrassed person moving the microphone away.

img.alt: Animation: a loop of four boxes with a dot racing around it: stronger sunlight adds about 30 degrees C (15 to 45); more evaporation and warm air holding more vapour; more water vapour, a greenhouse gas; stronger greenhouse, even hotter. Beside it a thermometer climbs while an ocean shrinks to nothing. End: oceans boil away, carbonate rocks release CO2, Earth becomes hotter than Venus.

steps.title: Move Earth to Venus's orbit
bullets: Stronger sunlight would quickly raise Earth's average temperature by about **30°C**, from 15°C to about 45°C, still below boiling.

More water would evaporate, and warmer air can hold more vapour. Water vapour is a greenhouse gas, so the greenhouse strengthens and the temperature climbs, which adds even more vapour: a self-reinforcing loop, a **runaway greenhouse effect**.

It would run until the oceans were gone and the carbonate rocks had released all their CO2, leaving Earth **hotter than Venus**. Then UV would split the water vapour and the hydrogen would escape: Earth would become another Venus.

img.alt: A timeline for Venus. About 4 billion years ago, with a fainter Sun, sunlight on Venus was about like Earth's today: rain, oceans, maybe life were possible. As the Sun brightened, a runaway greenhouse evaporated the water, ultraviolet split it and the hydrogen escaped. Today any ocean is gone and resurfacing has erased the evidence.

steps.title: A pleasant early Venus?
bullets: Venus is only about **30% closer** to the Sun, but that was critical: Earth was cool enough for rain and oceans that locked CO2 in rock; on Venus oceans either never formed or soon evaporated.
About 4 billion years ago the young Sun was dimmer, and sunlight on Venus was not much stronger than on Earth today, so rain, oceans and even life might have existed.

As the Sun brightened, the runaway greenhouse evaporated the water, UV split it and the hydrogen escaped. Global repaving by tectonics and volcanism has erased any shorelines, so we may never know for sure. Had Earth formed a bit closer to the Sun, it might have met the same fate.

boxes.text: Water vapour is both the result of warming and a cause of more warming, so once evaporation outpaces rain the loop feeds itself.
Runaway loop: Hotter, more vapour, hotter, more vapour... until the oceans are gone.

The runaway starts well BELOW boiling (about 45°C), because warmer air holds more water vapour (Book 10.5, p. 301). Moving Venus to Earth's orbit would NOT make it Earth-like: its water is already gone (Think About It, p. 302). 'Positive' feedback means self-reinforcing, not 'good' (p. 301).

As the Sun brightened, a runaway greenhouse evaporated the water, ultraviolet split it and the hydrogen escaped. Today any ocean is gone and resurfacing has erased the evidence.

sections.title: How Earth's atmosphere became unique

img.alt: Four cards. Water: Earth was cool enough for vapour to rain into oceans, maybe 4.3-4.4 billion years ago. Carbon dioxide: the oceans dissolved it into carbonate rocks. Nitrogen and oxygen: nitrogen was the volcanic gas left behind, oxygen comes from life. Stratosphere: life's oxygen made ozone, which absorbs ultraviolet.

steps.title: Four questions
bullets: Earth's nitrogen-oxygen air gives just enough warmth and pressure for water to exist as ice, liquid and vapour, shields us from harmful solar radiation and makes our weather.

Outgassing should have released the same gases on Venus, Earth and Mars, so why is Earth's air different? Four questions: why Earth kept its water; why it has so little CO2; why its air is mostly N₂ and O₂; and why it has an ultraviolet-absorbing stratosphere.

**Water**: on Mars some was split by UV and the rest froze; on Venus it was too hot to condense, so nearly all was split and the hydrogen escaped. Earth was **cool enough for vapour to rain into oceans**, perhaps as early as 4.3-4.4 billion years ago (from tiny mineral grains).

img.alt: Three bars on a stretched scale comparing Earth's carbon dioxide with the amount in the air: atmosphere 1; dissolved in the oceans about 60 times as much; in carbonate rocks about 170,000 times as much. Note: if all of it were in the air, Earth would be nearly as hot as Venus.

steps.title: Carbon dioxide went into the sea and rocks
bullets: Most of Earth's outgassed CO2 dissolved in the oceans, where chemical reactions turned it into carbonate rocks.
Even today the oceans hold about **60 times** as much CO2 as the air, and carbonate rocks about **170,000 times** as much.
**Nitrogen** (78%) is easy: it is the third most common volcanic gas after water vapour and CO2. With the water in oceans and the CO2 in rocks, nitrogen was left as the main gas.

img.alt: Ocean and land below, an ozone band on top. Green arrows rise from ocean life and land plants: photosynthesis takes in carbon dioxide and releases oxygen. Ultraviolet turns some oxygen into ozone, which absorbs ultraviolet and shields the surface. Note: fire, rust and browning fruit remove oxygen; without life it would be gone in a few million years.

steps.title: Oxygen and ozone come from life
bullets: Oxygen (21%) is a puzzle: molecular oxygen is not made by outgassing or any geological process, and it is highly reactive. Fire, rust and browning cut fruit are **oxidation reactions** that remove it; similar reactions redden rocks such as those of the Grand Canyon.
Without constant replacement, oxygen would vanish in a few million years. The answer is **life**: photosynthesis takes in CO2 and releases O₂.

It took at least a billion years of photosynthesis before oxygen began to build up, and there has probably been enough to breathe only for the past few hundred million years. Today life adds oxygen about as fast as animals and chemical reactions use it.

Ultraviolet turns some O₂ into **ozone (O₃)**, which absorbs UV even better, heats the upper air to make the **stratosphere** and shields the surface. Mars and Venus lack photosynthetic life, so they have too little O₂ and ozone for a stratosphere.

steps.title: Ozone: good or bad?
bullets: Near the ground, ozone is a main ingredient of urban smog from cars and industry, and it is poisonous to most living things.

High in the stratosphere, natural ozone is a vital shield against solar ultraviolet. That is why chemicals that destroy it, such as **CFCs** (chlorofluorocarbons), have been a serious environmental problem.

boxes.text: Liquid water is the hinge: oceans saved the water from UV, pulled out the CO2 and let life arise, and life then made the oxygen and ozone.
Earth's air recipe: water to the oceans, CO2 to the rocks, N₂ left over, O₂ from life, O₃ from O₂.

Oxygen does NOT come from volcanoes or any geological process; only life makes it (Book 10.6, p. 302). Nitrogen is only the third most common volcanic gas; it dominates because water and CO2 were removed (p. 302). Ground-level ozone is a pollutant even though stratospheric ozone protects us (Common Misconceptions, p. 303).

sections.title: The CO2 cycle: Earth's thermostat

img.alt: Animation of a carbon atom travelling around a loop: 1, carbon dioxide dissolves in rain making a mild acid; 2, the rain wears down rock and rivers carry minerals to the sea; 3, the minerals and dissolved CO2 form carbonate rock such as limestone; 4, plate tectonics carries it down at a subduction zone; 5, it melts and frees the CO2; 6, volcanoes outgas it again.

steps.title: The cycle
bullets: Earth's climate has stayed in the range for liquid water for about 4 billion years, even though the Sun has brightened about 30%. The greenhouse effect must adjust itself. The mechanism is the **carbon dioxide (CO2) cycle**:
Atmospheric CO2 dissolves in **rainwater**, making a mild acid. The acid rain wears down rock on the continents and **rivers** carry the minerals to the sea.

In the oceans, calcium from those minerals combines with dissolved CO2 and settles to the floor as **carbonate rock** such as limestone (in the last half billion years mostly as seashells; before that by chemistry alone).
Over millions of years **plate tectonics** carries the carbonate rock to subduction zones; deep down some of it melts and releases its CO2, which **volcanoes** outgas back into the air.

img.alt: Two chains of boxes. Too warm: more evaporation and rain, more CO2 dissolved and turned into carbonate rock, less CO2 in the air, weaker greenhouse, Earth cools. Too cool: less rain, less CO2 removed, volcanic CO2 builds up, stronger greenhouse, Earth warms. Note: far too slow to cause or fix today's rapid change.

steps.title: Self-regulating feedback
bullets: The rate at which CO2 is pulled out of the air rises with temperature.
**Too warm**: more evaporation and rain, so more CO2 dissolves and forms carbonates; atmospheric CO2 falls, the greenhouse weakens and Earth cools back.
**Too cool**: less rain, so less CO2 is removed; volcanic CO2 builds up, the greenhouse strengthens and Earth warms back.
The cycle takes **hundreds of thousands of years** to stabilize CO2. It works on geological time scales, so it is neither the cause of nor the cure for today's rapid change.

boxes.text: The thermostat works because the CO2 'removal' step (rain and rock weathering) speeds up when it is warm and slows down when it is cool, while volcanoes keep adding CO2 at a steady pace.
Rain, Rivers, Rock, Recycle (subduction), Release (volcanoes).

The CO2 cycle is SELF-REGULATING (negative feedback), the opposite of a runaway (Book 10.6, p. 304). It is far too slow to remove the CO2 people are adding now (p. 304). Plate tectonics is essential: without subduction the carbonate rock would never return its CO2 (Figure 10.36).

sections.title: Ice ages, snowball Earth and the far future

steps.title: Ice ages
bullets: Earth's climate still varies because the CO2 cycle is slow to respond.

An **ice age** comes when the global average temperature drops by just a few degrees: more snow falls and ice spreads to fairly low latitudes. The northern United States was buried in glaciers at the peak of the last ice age, which ended only about **12,000 years** ago.

Over tens to hundreds of millions of years, the brightening Sun and moving continents influence climate. Over the past few million years, ice ages seem driven mainly by **Milankovitch cycles**, small changes in tilt, rotation and orbit, amplified by greenhouse feedbacks into ice ages and warmer **interglacial** periods.

img.alt: A cycle of five boxes around an icy Earth: a long cold spell starts freezing the oceans; ice reflects up to about 90% of sunlight, more cooling, a snowball; ice-covered oceans cannot take up CO2 so volcanic CO2 builds up; the strong greenhouse melts the ice and dark water absorbs more, a hothouse; the CO2 cycle restarts and returns to normal.

steps.title: Snowball Earth
bullets: Between about **750 and 580 million years ago**, glaciers may have reached the equator. Ice reflects up to about 90% of sunlight, so more ice meant more cooling: a self-reinforcing plunge into a **snowball Earth** (some models say -50°C, oceans frozen a kilometre or more deep; others say a slushy 'slushball').

Escape: Earth's interior heat kept volcanoes outgassing CO2, and ice-covered oceans could not absorb it. After perhaps 10 million years the greenhouse melted the ice; dark water absorbed more sunlight and Earth swung into a **hothouse**, perhaps over 50°C, within a few centuries. The CO2 cycle then restored balance over hundreds of thousands of years.
The end of these episodes roughly coincides with the **Cambrian explosion** of life; the harsh conditions may have spurred evolution.

img.alt: A timeline (not to scale): for 4 billion years Earth kept liquid water although the Sun brightened about 30%; snowball Earth episodes 750-580 million years ago; the last ice age ended 12,000 years ago; in about a billion years the warming Sun may start removing water; in 3-4 billion years sunlight will be as strong as on Venus today and a runaway greenhouse follows.

steps.title: The far future
bullets: Earth's climate has stayed suitable for life for some 4 billion years, but the Sun keeps brightening.
Some models say Earth could start losing its water in about **a billion years**; others say the CO2 cycle could hold on longer.

By about **3 to 4 billion years** from now sunlight on Earth will be as strong as on Venus today: a runaway greenhouse will make Earth a Venus-like hothouse. So Earth stays habitable for somewhere between 1 and 4 billion more years.

boxes.text: Ice is both a result of cold and a cause of more cold, because it reflects sunlight; that self-reinforcing loop can tip Earth into a snowball.
Snowball to hothouse: volcanoes never stop, so CO2 always wins in the end.

Earth escaped snowball phases because volcanic CO2 built up, not because the Sun suddenly brightened (Book 10.6, p. 305). The last ice age ended about 12,000 years ago, not millions (p. 305). The far-future runaway greenhouse is 1-4 billion years away, not a near-term threat (p. 306).

sections.title: The evidence for human-caused warming

img.alt: Two boxes joined by arrows to a conclusion. Fact 1: carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases trap heat. Fact 2: human activity, mainly burning coal, oil and gas, is adding a lot more of them. Conclusion: warming is inevitable, and measurements show it is happening.

steps.title: Simple basic science
bullets: Past rapid changes (several degrees in decades, sea level up or down tens of metres) had natural causes: orbit and tilt changes, big eruptions, CO2 released from oceans. Today's change has a new cause: **human activity** is rapidly raising CO2 and other greenhouse gases.
**Fact 1**: CO2 and other greenhouse gases trap heat, making a world warmer than it would otherwise be (shown by laboratory measurements and planetary studies).
**Fact 2**: human activity, especially burning fossil fuels (coal, oil and gas), is adding much more CO2 and other greenhouse gases to the air.
**Inevitable conclusion**: global warming must follow. The global average temperature has already risen by about **1.1°C** (the 2021 IPCC report: 0.8 to 1.3°C caused by people).

img.alt: Sketch of carbon dioxide over the past 800,000 years: a blue line rising and falling in long cycles but never above about 280 parts per million, then a red line shooting straight up to over 420 ppm today. Note: low CO2 matches ice ages, high CO2 warm interglacial periods; temperature rises and falls with CO2.

steps.title: The CO2 record
bullets: Air bubbles trapped in **Antarctic ice cores** record CO2 for the past 800,000 years; direct measurements began in the late 1950s (Charles Keeling, so the graph is called the **Keeling curve**).
For 800,000 years CO2 **never exceeded about 280 parts per million (ppm)** until the industrial age began around 1750. It is now **over 420 ppm**, a rise of more than 50%, and still climbing fast.
CO2 and temperature have risen and fallen **together** throughout those 800,000 years: low CO2 with ice ages, high CO2 with warm interglacials.

img.alt: Three cards. 1, the amounts match: human CO2 release has risen in step with the concentration and a little under half of it stays in the air, while natural sources give only about 1% of what is needed. 2, oxygen in the air is dropping slightly, as burning fuel predicts. 3, the carbon isotope mix has shifted toward that of fossil fuels.

steps.title: Proof the extra CO2 is ours
bullets: **1. The amounts match.** Human CO2 emissions have risen in step with the concentration and easily account for it; a little less than half stays in the air and the rest goes into the oceans and ground. Natural sources such as volcanoes and the oceans supply only about **1%** of what would be needed.
**2. Oxygen is dropping.** Burning fossil fuels uses oxygen, and the expected small drop in oxygen in the air and oceans is measured.

**3. The carbon fingerprint.** The ratio of carbon-12, carbon-13 and carbon-14 in atmospheric CO2 has shifted in a way explained only by adding carbon with the distinctive isotope mix of **fossil fuels**. Perhaps the most convincing evidence of all.

img.alt: Sketch of global temperature since 1850: a jagged black observed line rising to about plus 1.1 degrees C, a purple line for models that include human greenhouse gases following it closely, and a flat green line for models with only the Sun and volcanoes that does not match the rise.

steps.title: Models confirm it
bullets: Climate models are computer simulations of Earth. Models that include **only natural factors** (changes in the Sun's brightness and volcanoes) do not match the temperatures measured since 1850.
Models that **also include the human greenhouse gases** match the data remarkably well.

So scientists are nearly unanimous: humans are causing the current warming. Without rapid, dramatic changes, people alive by the end of this century will live in the warmest climate any generation of Homo sapiens has known.

The idea is old: in 1896 Svante Arrhenius calculated that doubling CO2 would warm Earth by about 5°C and that burning coal already added about as much CO2 each year as volcanoes; Eunice Newton Foote had studied the greenhouse effect 40 years before. Modern models agree with him: a few degrees for a doubling.

boxes.text: The argument has two independent legs: the physics (greenhouse gases trap heat) and the measurements (we are adding them and the world is warming as predicted).
Three fingerprints of our CO2: the Amount matches, the Oxygen drops, the Isotopes point to fossil fuels (A-O-I).

The greenhouse effect itself is NOT bad: without it Earth would freeze; the problem is too much of it, as Venus shows (Book 10.6, Common Misconceptions, p. 306). Volcanoes supply only about 1% of the CO2 needed to explain the rise (p. 307). Only a little less than half of our CO2 stays in the air (p. 307).

sections.title: Consequences and solutions

img.alt: Sketch of warming from 1950 to 2100: an observed black line to today, then three paths: low (green) staying under a dashed 2 degree C line, intermediate (amber) and high (red) climbing above it. Note: only the low path, with fast deep cuts in emissions, stays under 2 degrees.

steps.title: How much more warming?
bullets: Models predict future warming along low, intermediate and high pathways, depending on how much greenhouse gas we keep adding.
Most scientists argue warming should stay below about **2°C**. Only the **low** pathway does that, and it needs an almost immediate, dramatic cut in CO2 emissions.
Climate **tipping points** could worsen things, such as warming releasing CO2 and methane trapped in Arctic **permafrost**.

img.alt: Five cards: 1, regional weather changes, with warmer nights and winters, more extreme heat, droughts in some places and floods in others; 2, stronger and more frequent extreme weather; 3, melting Arctic sea ice, which also lets dark water absorb more heat; 4, rising sea level; 5, ocean acidification from dissolved CO2 harming coral reefs and fisheries.

steps.title: Five kinds of consequences
bullets: Almost every region is warmer than a few decades ago, but some (especially the Arctic) much more: that is why we speak of **climate change**, not just warming.
**1. Regional weather changes**: nights warm more than days and winters more than summers; more extreme summer heat; some regions drier (drought, wildfire), others wetter (floods).
**2. More extreme weather**: more heat and energy in the lower air and oceans drive stronger or more frequent hurricanes, floods, droughts, heat waves and even winter storms.

**3. Melting sea ice**: Arctic ice is shrinking fast and summers may be ice-free by about mid-century. It hurts polar bears, freshens the sea (possibly changing currents) and, since ice reflects more than open water, amplifies the warming.

**5. Ocean acidification**: roughly **30%** of human CO2 dissolves in the oceans and makes them more acidic; with the warming, it has been tied to dying coral reefs and less productive fisheries. (Number 4, sea level, is next.)

img.alt: Three bars on a stretched scale: past century or so, more than 20 cm of sea level rise; by 2100 on intermediate paths, close to 1 m, enough to flood much of Florida; if all polar ice melted, about 70 m over centuries to millennia. Causes: warm water expands and land ice melts; melting sea ice barely changes sea level.

steps.title: Rising sea level
bullets: Two causes: water **expands slightly as it warms**, and melting land ice, especially from **Greenland and Antarctica**, adds water. Melting sea ice barely matters, because it was already floating.

Sea level has already risen more than **20 cm** in about a century. Intermediate scenarios give close to **1 m** by 2100, enough to flood much of Florida; melting all polar ice would raise it about **70 m**, over centuries or millennia.
'Consequences of consequences' are possible too, such as fresh meltwater changing the Gulf Stream, or losses of forests and biodiversity.

img.alt: Two boxes joined by an arrow. Step 1, stop adding greenhouse gases: efficiency, wind and solar, nuclear, and later perhaps fusion or solar power from space. Step 2, take carbon dioxide back out: plant trees and store carbon in soil, and machines that capture CO2 from the air. One suggested goal: bring CO2 back to about 350 ppm.

steps.title: A solvable problem
bullets: Because the cause is our greenhouse gas emissions, cutting them slows or stops the warming, and the technology exists: better efficiency, renewables such as wind and solar, and nuclear power.
Future options include **nuclear fusion** (the ITER project in France aims to demonstrate it), new kinds of fission that recycle nuclear waste, and solar power collected in space.

Stopping emissions does not undo the damage already done, so a second step is **removing CO2**: passively (more trees, farming that stores carbon in soil) and actively (machines capturing CO2 from the air, which need lots of energy). One suggested target is about **350 ppm**.

boxes.text: Small changes in the global average shift the whole range of weather, so 'normal' summers of today were 'hot' summers a few decades ago.
Five consequences: Weather, Wild storms, Waning sea ice, Water rising, Wrecked reefs (acid oceans).

Melting SEA ice does not raise sea level much (it already floats); melting LAND ice and warm water expanding do (Book 10.6, pp. 309-310). Only the low pathway stays under 2°C (p. 308). Ending emissions alone does not reverse damage already done; CO2 must also be removed (p. 311).

The average of weather over many years.
A huge loop of air: warm air rises at the equator and flows poleward aloft; cool air sinks and returns along the surface. Also called a Hadley cell.
cards.short: Loop of air carrying heat poleward

cards.back: The sideways drift of moving air on a rotating planet: to the right in the Northern Hemisphere and to the left in the Southern.

cards.front: Which way do Northern Hemisphere storms spin?
cards.back: Counterclockwise around a low-pressure centre (clockwise in the Southern Hemisphere).

cards.front: How many circulation cells per hemisphere on Earth?
cards.back: Three. The Coriolis effect splits the single cell that a non-rotating Earth would have.

cards.front: What makes the Coriolis effect stronger?
cards.back: Larger planet size and faster rotation. Venus's is very weak (slow spin); Mars's is weak (small size).
Rain, snow and hail. It needs clouds, which form when water vapour condenses.
Extreme sensitivity of a chaotic system to its starting conditions: a tiny change can make a long-range forecast completely different.

cards.front: Why are there deserts at 20-30° latitude?
cards.back: Equatorial rain wrings the moisture out of the air, and the circulation cells carry that dry air to 20-30° where it sinks.
cards.short: Dried air from the cells sinks there

cards.back: The Sun's slow brightening with age: about 30% brighter now than when the solar system was young.

cards.back: Pitch black around the bright Sun, because there is too little gas to scatter light.

quiz.q: If Earth did not rotate, how would air circulate between the equator and the poles?
options: Winds would blow only east to west at every latitude
One large cell per hemisphere: air rises at the poles and sinks at the equator
Three cells per hemisphere, as it does today
Air would not circulate, because rotation is what moves it
One large cell per hemisphere: air rises at the equator and sinks at the poles
quiz.why: Heating alone drives warm equatorial air up and poleward, and cool polar air down and back along the surface: one cell per hemisphere. Rotation (the Coriolis effect) is what splits each one into three.
