quiz.q: Which statement about the Coriolis effect is NOT correct?
options: It decides which way water swirls down a sink
It is stronger on larger, faster-rotating planets
It makes moving air turn right in the Northern Hemisphere
It splits Earth's circulation into three cells per hemisphere
It makes storms spin opposite ways in the two hemispheres
quiz.why: The Coriolis effect matters only when material moves hundreds of kilometres toward or away from the rotation axis. For a sink it is negligible; the bowl's shape and the water's starting motion decide.

img.alt: Left: a hurricane hundreds of kilometres across whose spin is set by the Coriolis effect. Right: a small sink drain under a metre across, where the Coriolis effect is far too weak; the bowl's shape and how the water started moving decide which way it swirls.

quiz.q: You are in the Northern Hemisphere and launch a long-range missile at a target 5,000 km due north. To hit it you should aim:
options: Directly at the target
Somewhat to the left (west)
Somewhat to the right (east)
Higher, but straight at the target
It depends on the time of day
quiz.why: Moving away from the equator, the missile keeps its faster eastward speed and gets ahead of the ground, curving to the right (east). Aiming somewhat left makes up for it.

quiz.q: Why do surface winds at mid-latitudes (30-60°) blow from west to east?
options: Earth's magnetic field pushes the air eastward
Surface air there flows toward the equator and is turned eastward
The Sun heats the western side of continents first
Mountain ranges steer the winds eastward
Surface air there flows poleward, and the Coriolis effect turns it eastward
quiz.why: In the mid-latitude cells the surface air moves toward the poles; the Coriolis effect diverts it into eastward winds. In the cells nearest the equator and the poles the surface air flows toward the equator and becomes westward winds.

img.alt: A globe with three loops of circulating air in each hemisphere, split at about 30 and 60 degrees latitude. Labels: high latitudes 60-90 degrees, winds blow east to west; mid-latitudes 30-60 degrees, winds blow west to east; near the equator 0-30 degrees, winds blow east to west. The Coriolis effect turns north-south flow into east-west winds.

quiz.q: Earth has rainforests near the equator and deserts near 20-30° latitude mainly because:
options: Strong equatorial convection rains out the moisture and the cells carry the dry air to 20-30°
The equator is closest to the Sun all year
Winds at 20-30° blow straight from the poles
The deserts lie in the rain shadow of the jungles' trees
The oceans are warmer at 20-30° than at the equator
quiz.why: More sunlight at the equator drives more convection and rain. That rain depletes the air of moisture, and the circulation cells carry it away to 20-30°, where little is left to fall.

img.alt: A green globe with a dark green rainy band at the equator and sandy bands at about 25 degrees north and south. Notes: the equator gets the most sunlight and convection, so lots of rain and jungles; the cells carry the dried-out air away and it sinks at 20-30 degrees, making deserts; summer afternoon convection brings thunderstorms.

quiz.q: Weather can be forecast only about a week ahead, yet climate models give reliable long-term predictions. Why?
options: Climate models use completely different physical laws
Climate is an average, and the chaotic details average out
Climate never changes, so it is easy to predict
Weather forecasts use too few computers
The butterfly effect only applies to climate, not weather
quiz.why: Weather is chaotic: tiny changes in starting conditions grow over time (the butterfly effect). Climate is the long-term average of weather, so those unpredictable details tend to cancel out.
quiz.source: Book 10.2, p. 289 (Special Topic: Weather and Chaos)

img.alt: Animation of a graph over 30 days with two forecast lines, blue and red, that start almost the same, stay together for the first few days and then wander completely apart by a month. A grey band marks the long-term average, which stays predictable: climate models remain reliable even when weather cannot be forecast.

quiz.q: Which change would tend to make Earth WARMER?
options: Ice caps growing larger
Volcanic aerosols reaching the stratosphere
More smog particles in the air
Arctic sea ice melting into open water
Cutting down large areas of forest
quiz.why: Open water reflects much less sunlight than ice, so Earth absorbs more and warms. Growing ice, aerosols, smog and deforestation all raise reflectivity and tend to cool.

img.alt: Four cards. Reflect more and cool: ice and snow, more clouds, volcanic dust. Reflect less and warm: open water where sea ice was, shrinking ice caps. People raise reflectivity with smog and by cutting forests. People lower it with roads and cities and by melting Arctic sea ice.

quiz.q: Suppose Earth's axis tilt increased from 23.5° to 25°. The most likely result would be:
options: Milder seasons and more ice, so a cooler Earth
More extreme seasons and less ice, so a slightly warmer Earth
No change, because tilt does not affect climate
Shorter years
A runaway greenhouse effect
quiz.why: Greater tilt means warmer summers and colder winters. The extra summer warmth keeps ice from building up, which lowers reflectivity and warms the planet overall.

img.alt: Animation: Earth's tilted axis rocks slowly back and forth while a label counts between 22 and 25 degrees (today about 23.5). Cards: more tilt brings hotter summers and colder winters and less ice, so warmer overall; less tilt lets ice build up, cooler, matching past ice ages; these Milankovitch cycles come from small gravity tugs.

quiz.q: Which pair of processes removes gas from an atmosphere PERMANENTLY?
options: Thermal escape and solar wind stripping
Condensation and chemical reactions
Outgassing and vaporization
Condensation and thermal escape
Chemical reactions and solar wind stripping
quiz.why: Thermal escape and solar wind stripping send gas into space. Condensation and chemical reactions only move gas to the surface or interior, and could be reversed if conditions change.

img.alt: Four cards in two columns. Can be undone: condensation, gas falling back as rain, snow or frost such as dry ice on Mars; chemical reactions, gas locked into rock or metal like rust. Permanent: thermal escape, fast particles reaching escape velocity; solar wind stripping where there is no magnetosphere.

quiz.q: If the temperature of a gas is multiplied by 4 (in kelvin), its peak thermal velocity is:
options: Multiplied by 16
Multiplied by 4
Halved
Multiplied by 2
Unchanged
quiz.why: v_thermal = √(2kT/m), so the speed grows with the square root of T: √4 = 2.

img.alt: The formula v thermal equals the square root of 2kT over m, where T is temperature in kelvin, m the mass of one particle and k is 1.38 x 10^-23 joule per kelvin. Cards: four times the temperature doubles the speed; four times the mass halves it. Rule of thumb: a gas faster than about 20% of escape velocity is lost within a few billion years.

quiz.q: A gas in a planet's exosphere has a peak thermal velocity equal to 40% of the planet's escape velocity. According to the rule of thumb, the gas will:
options: Never escape, because 40% is below 100%
Escape only if the planet has no magnetic field
Condense onto the surface instead
Escape only during impacts
Be completely lost within a few billion years
quiz.why: A peak thermal velocity above about 20% of escape velocity lets a gas be lost completely within a few billion years, because the fast tail of the speed distribution keeps leaking away.

img.alt: Graph of how many sodium atoms in the Moon's 400 K exosphere move at each speed: a hump peaking near 0.5 km/s (the peak thermal velocity) with a thin shaded tail beyond the escape velocity line at 2.4 km/s. Beside it, an animation of atoms bouncing above the ground while a few fast red ones fly off the top for good.

quiz.q: The Moon has a thin sodium exosphere but almost no hydrogen. Why?
options: Sodium is lighter than hydrogen
Hydrogen's thermal speed tops escape speed; sodium's does not
The Moon's volcanoes release sodium but not hydrogen
Hydrogen freezes onto the lunar surface
The solar wind adds sodium and removes nothing
quiz.why: At 400 K hydrogen peaks at about 2.6 km/s, above the Moon's 2.4 km/s escape velocity, so it leaves quickly. Sodium peaks near 0.5 km/s, escapes slowly, and surface ejection keeps replacing it.

img.alt: Bar chart of peak thermal speeds on the Moon at 400 K against its escape velocity of 2.4 km/s: hydrogen 2.6 km/s, past the line, so it escapes quickly; sodium 0.5 km/s, about 20% of escape, so it leaks slowly and is topped up from the surface.

quiz.q: Standing on the Moon at noon, what would you see?
options: A pale blue sky
A reddish-orange sky
A pitch-black sky around the bright Sun
A yellow-brown dusty sky
A white, overcast sky
quiz.why: The Moon's gas is far too thin to scatter sunlight, so the sky stays black even in daylight.

img.alt: A grey lunar landscape under a black sky with the bright Sun, labelled: black sky even in daylight, too little gas to scatter light. Cards: no absorption so no troposphere, stratosphere or thermosphere, only an exosphere; frozen, the whole atmosphere would almost fit in a dorm room; rare collisions let particles reach thousands of kilometres up.

quiz.q: Why are Mars's southern-hemisphere seasons more extreme than its northern ones?
options: Mars is closest to the Sun during southern summer because its orbit is elliptical
Its southern hemisphere has more tilt
The southern polar cap is made of dry ice
Dust storms only happen in the south
Jupiter's gravity warms the south
quiz.why: Mars's more elliptical orbit puts it significantly closer to the Sun in southern summer and farther in southern winter, giving short warm southern summers and long frigid southern winters.

img.alt: Mars's stretched orbit around an off-centre Sun. On the near side Mars is closer and moving fast: southern summer is short and warm while northern winter is short and mild. On the far side it is farther and slower: southern winter is long and frigid, northern summer long and cool.

quiz.q: Which statement about Mars's seasonal polar caps is correct?
options: Water vapour freezes at the winter pole while CO2 melts into lakes
Both caps are pure dry ice all year
CO2 freezes into dry ice at the winter pole and vaporizes at the summer pole, leaving a water-ice cap
The caps never change, because Mars has no seasons
Air pressure rises at the winter pole as gas freezes there
quiz.why: The winter pole reaches about -130°C and CO2 condenses there; the summer pole's dry ice vaporizes, leaving water ice. Pressure rises at the summer pole and falls at the winter pole; up to a third of the air moves.

img.alt: Animation of Mars through a year: the polar cap at the winter pole grows with frozen carbon dioxide while the summer cap shrinks to its water-ice core, and white arrows show wind blowing from the summer pole toward the winter pole. Notes: the winter pole reaches about -130 degrees C, and up to a third of the atmosphere moves pole to pole.

quiz.q: What would happen if Mars's axis tilt stayed close to 0° for tens of thousands of years?
options: The poles would warm and the atmosphere would thicken
Nothing would change, because Mars's tilt has no effect
Liquid water would become stable at the surface
Mars would develop a strong magnetic field
More CO2 would freeze at the poles, thinning the air and cooling the whole planet
quiz.why: With little tilt the poles stay in a deep freeze; more CO2 freezes out, lowering the pressure and weakening the greenhouse effect, so the entire planet cools.

img.alt: Animation: Mars's axis swings slowly from upright to tipped far over while a label counts from 0 to 60 degrees. Cards: a small tilt freezes CO2 at the poles, thinning the air and cooling Mars; a large tilt warms the summer pole and thickens the air; the swings are big because Jupiter tugs harder and the tiny moons cannot steady the axis.

quiz.q: Which is NOT a reason given for why Mars's axis tilt varies so much more than Earth's?
options: Jupiter's gravity has a greater effect on Mars
Mars's orbit is closer to Jupiter's
Phobos and Deimos are too small to steady its axis
Earth's axis is steadied by our large Moon
Mars spins much faster than Earth
quiz.why: The two reasons are Jupiter's stronger pull on Mars (its orbit is closer to Jupiter's) and the lack of a large stabilizing moon. Rotation speed is not one of them.

quiz.q: According to the leading hypothesis, Mars lost most of its carbon dioxide because:
options: It all froze into the polar caps
A runaway greenhouse boiled it away
Plate tectonics buried it deep inside the planet
Its cooling core stopped making a magnetic field, so the solar wind could strip the gas away
Its moons captured the gas
quiz.why: As small Mars cooled, core convection stopped and its magnetic field weakened. CO2 split into carbon and oxygen atoms that the solar wind stripped away. Some CO2 is in the caps and carbonate rocks, but most was probably lost to space.

img.alt: Mars with arrows of gas leaving into space toward the solar wind from the Sun. Labels: most of the carbon dioxide was lost to space, split into carbon and oxygen atoms and swept off by the solar wind once the magnetic field faded; some froze into the polar caps; some is locked into carbonate rocks.

quiz.q: Some people propose 'terraforming' Mars by releasing all the CO2 frozen in its polar caps. Based on where Mars's ancient atmosphere went, the best prediction is that:
options: The ancient thick atmosphere and oceans would fully return
Mars would undergo a runaway greenhouse like Venus
It would not restore the ancient atmosphere, because most of that CO2 was lost to space
It would trigger Mars's magnetic field again
The released CO2 would immediately escape by thermal escape
quiz.why: Only some of the old CO2 condensed into the caps; the bulk was probably lost to space, and most of the water is gone for good. The caps cannot rebuild the dense early atmosphere.

quiz.q: Deuterium is about 100 times more common, relative to ordinary hydrogen, on Venus than on Earth. This is evidence that Venus:
options: Was struck by deuterium-rich comets
Lost much water, as its lighter hydrogen escaped to space
Still has deep oceans under its crust
Has a strong magnetic field
Formed farther from the Sun than Earth
quiz.why: Deuterium is twice as heavy as hydrogen and escapes less easily. If much water was split and its hydrogen lost to space, the deuterium would be left behind, raising its share, as measured.

img.alt: Two boxes of hydrogen atoms (small white dots) with a few heavier deuterium atoms (larger purple dots). At the start there are many hydrogen atoms; after ultraviolet splits water and most hydrogen escapes, few hydrogen atoms remain but the deuterium is still there. Note: deuterium makes up about 100 times more of the hydrogen on Venus than on Earth.

quiz.q: Imagine Earth were moved to Venus's orbit. What would happen?
options: A 30°C warming, after which Earth would settle at about 45°C with its oceans intact
The CO2 cycle would quickly cool Earth back to 15°C
Earth would freeze because of extra cloud cover
A runaway greenhouse: oceans evaporate, carbonate rocks release their CO2, and Earth ends up hotter than Venus
Nothing, because distance from the Sun does not matter
quiz.why: More evaporation adds water vapour, a greenhouse gas, which warms Earth further and adds more vapour: a self-reinforcing loop that would boil off the oceans and free the CO2 in rocks.

img.alt: Animation: a loop of four boxes with a dot racing around it: stronger sunlight adds about 30 degrees C (15 to 45); more evaporation and warm air holding more vapour; more water vapour, a greenhouse gas; stronger greenhouse, even hotter. Beside it a thermometer climbs while an ocean shrinks to nothing. End: oceans boil away, carbonate rocks release CO2, Earth becomes hotter than Venus.

quiz.q: Earth outgassed about as much carbon dioxide as Venus. Where is most of Earth's CO2 now?
options: Locked in carbonate rocks such as limestone
Lost to space by thermal escape
In the atmosphere
Frozen in the polar ice caps
Used up by animals breathing
quiz.why: CO2 dissolved in the oceans and chemical reactions turned it into carbonate rocks, which hold about 170,000 times as much CO2 as the atmosphere (the oceans hold about 60 times as much).

img.alt: Three bars on a stretched scale comparing Earth's carbon dioxide with the amount in the air: atmosphere 1; dissolved in the oceans about 60 times as much; in carbonate rocks about 170,000 times as much. Note: if all of it were in the air, Earth would be nearly as hot as Venus.

quiz.q: Suppose all photosynthetic life on Earth died out. What would happen to the oxygen in our atmosphere?
options: Nothing; volcanoes would keep replacing it
It would turn into nitrogen
It would slowly be removed by chemical reactions such as rusting, over a few million years
It would immediately escape to space
It would double, since nothing would use it
quiz.why: Oxygen is not made by outgassing or any geological process, and reactions like fire, rust and oxidation of rock keep removing it. Without photosynthesis to replace it, it would be gone in just a few million years.

img.alt: Ocean and land below, an ozone band on top. Green arrows rise from ocean life and land plants: photosynthesis takes in carbon dioxide and releases oxygen. Ultraviolet turns some oxygen into ozone, which absorbs ultraviolet and shields the surface. Note: fire, rust and browning fruit remove oxygen; without life it would be gone in a few million years.

quiz.q: Earth warms slightly for natural reasons. How does the carbon dioxide cycle respond?
options: Volcanoes release more CO2, warming Earth further
The oceans release their CO2, causing a runaway greenhouse
More rain dissolves more CO2 into carbonate rocks, lowering atmospheric CO2 and cooling Earth
Nothing happens, because the cycle does not depend on temperature
Plate tectonics stops, trapping CO2 in the interior
quiz.why: Warmer temperatures mean more evaporation and rainfall, so more CO2 dissolves and forms carbonate rocks. Atmospheric CO2 drops, the greenhouse weakens and Earth cools: self-regulating feedback.

img.alt: Two chains of boxes. Too warm: more evaporation and rain, more CO2 dissolved and turned into carbonate rock, less CO2 in the air, weaker greenhouse, Earth cools. Too cool: less rain, less CO2 removed, volcanic CO2 builds up, stronger greenhouse, Earth warms. Note: far too slow to cause or fix today's rapid change.

quiz.q: How did Earth escape from its 'snowball' episodes?
options: The Sun suddenly brightened
Large asteroid impacts melted the ice
Volcanoes kept outgassing CO2, which built up because ice-covered oceans could not absorb it
Earth's axis tilt dropped to zero
Life produced enough oxygen to warm the planet
quiz.why: The cold surface did not affect Earth's interior heat, so volcanoes kept adding CO2. With the oceans iced over, it accumulated until the greenhouse effect melted the ice, even overshooting into a 'hothouse'.

img.alt: A cycle of five boxes around an icy Earth: a long cold spell starts freezing the oceans; ice reflects up to about 90% of sunlight, more cooling, a snowball; ice-covered oceans cannot take up CO2 so volcanic CO2 builds up; the strong greenhouse melts the ice and dark water absorbs more, a hothouse; the CO2 cycle restarts and returns to normal.

quiz.q: Which is NOT one of the lines of evidence that the recent rise in CO2 comes from human activity?
options: Human CO2 emissions have risen in step with the concentration
Oxygen in the air is decreasing slightly
The carbon isotope mix matches that of fossil fuels
Volcanoes have been erupting much more CO2 than before
Natural sources could supply only about 1% of the rise
quiz.why: Natural sources such as volcanoes and the oceans supply only about 1% of what would be needed. The evidence is the matching amounts, the slight drop in oxygen from burning, and the fossil-fuel carbon isotope signature.

img.alt: Three cards. 1, the amounts match: human CO2 release has risen in step with the concentration and a little under half of it stays in the air, while natural sources give only about 1% of what is needed. 2, oxygen in the air is dropping slightly, as burning fuel predicts. 3, the carbon isotope mix has shifted toward that of fossil fuels.

quiz.q: CO2 never exceeded about 280 ppm for 800,000 years but is now above 420 ppm. By about what percentage has it increased?
options: About 15%
About 33%
About 100%
About 50%
About 150%
quiz.why: (420 - 280) / 280 = 140 / 280 = 0.5, an increase of about 50% since the industrial age began around 1750.

img.alt: Sketch of carbon dioxide over the past 800,000 years: a blue line rising and falling in long cycles but never above about 280 parts per million, then a red line shooting straight up to over 420 ppm today. Note: low CO2 matches ice ages, high CO2 warm interglacial periods; temperature rises and falls with CO2.

quiz.q: Climate models that include only natural factors (the Sun and volcanoes) are compared with models that also include human greenhouse gases. What do the results show?
options: Only the models that include the human contribution match the measured temperatures
Both match the observed warming equally well
Only the natural-factor models match the data
Neither matches, so models are not useful
The models predict cooling since 1850
quiz.why: Models ignoring the human contribution do not match the data, but the full models including human greenhouse gases match the measured temperatures remarkably well.

img.alt: Sketch of global temperature since 1850: a jagged black observed line rising to about plus 1.1 degrees C, a purple line for models that include human greenhouse gases following it closely, and a flat green line for models with only the Sun and volcanoes that does not match the rise.

quiz.q: Melting Arctic sea ice does NOT raise sea level much. Why is it still a concern for climate?
options: It releases large amounts of CO2
It slows Earth's rotation
It makes the oceans saltier
It thickens the ozone layer
Open water absorbs more sunlight than ice does
quiz.why: Sea ice already floats, so melting it barely changes sea level. But replacing reflective ice with dark open water amplifies warming; the fresh meltwater can also affect currents and fisheries.

img.alt: Five cards: 1, regional weather changes, with warmer nights and winters, more extreme heat, droughts in some places and floods in others; 2, stronger and more frequent extreme weather; 3, melting Arctic sea ice, which also lets dark water absorb more heat; 4, rising sea level; 5, ocean acidification from dissolved CO2 harming coral reefs and fisheries.

quiz.q: Venus takes 243 Earth days to rotate once. Which description of its weather follows from that slow spin?
options: A strong Coriolis effect that splits its circulation into many small cells
A very weak Coriolis effect: little surface wind, no hurricane-like storms and just two large circulation cells
A huge temperature difference between day and night
Violent hurricanes that circle the planet every 4 days at ground level
Strong seasons caused by its 177° axis tilt
quiz.why: Slow rotation means a very weak Coriolis effect, so Venus has little surface wind, never any hurricane-like storms, and only two large cells. Its thick air keeps day and night equally hot; the 4-day winds are high in the clouds; and 177° tilt means virtually no tilt, so no seasons.

img.alt: Two bands. High up, about 400 degrees C cooler than the ground: sulfuric acid clouds, acid rain that evaporates at least 30 km above the surface, winds that circle the planet in 4 days. At the surface: slow 243-day rotation, weak Coriolis effect, winds of a few km/h, no storms or rain. Cards: two big cells, same temperature everywhere, no seasons.

quiz.q: Which of the following best describes the nature and origin of the atmospheres of the Moon and Mercury?
options: They have thin atmospheres produced by outgassing, but still have the layers of a troposphere, thermosphere, and exosphere.
They have thin exospheres only, with gas coming from impacts of subatomic particles and photons.
They have only small amounts of gas, all of which is left over from outgassing long ago.
They have thin tropospheres only, with gas coming from vaporization.
quiz.why: The Moon and Mercury have only extremely thin exospheres. Their gas is knocked off the surface by micrometeorites, solar wind particles and high-energy solar photons (surface ejection).

quiz.q: Which of the following describes a primary role of global circulation cells in a planet's atmosphere?
options: They create severe weather such as thunderstorms.
They cause air to be diverted into hurricane-like swirls.
They transport heat from the equator toward the poles.
They keep the poles cold enough to have polar caps.
quiz.why: Circulation cells carry heat from the warm equator toward the cooler poles: warm air rises at the equator, moves poleward high up, cools, sinks and flows back near the surface.

quiz.q: What is the Coriolis effect?
options: A law of physics that explains why toilets flush the opposite way in Australia.
An effect involving straight-line motion being perceived as curved because the observer is rotating.
An effect that involves objects' trajectories curving on the surface of the Earth due to the atmosphere.
An effect that involves airborne spinning objects curving their trajectories in the direction of their rotation.
quiz.why: On a rotating surface (a merry-go-round or a spinning planet), something moving in a straight line appears to curve to an observer turning with the surface.

quiz.q: Which of the following is not caused by the Coriolis effect on Earth?
options: Hurricanes swirl in opposite directions in the Northern and Southern hemispheres.
Water going down a drain swirls in opposite directions in the Northern and Southern hemispheres.
Air or objects moving northward in the Northern Hemisphere are deflected to the east.
Earth's global circulation cells are split into three separate cells in each hemisphere.
quiz.why: The Coriolis effect only matters over large distances. A sink or toilet is far too small, so its swirl is set by its shape and how the water entered, not by hemisphere.

quiz.q: Venus experiences the Coriolis effect, but it is much weaker compared to Earth. Which of the following explains why this is the case?
options: Venus has a much thicker atmosphere
Venus is much hotter
Venus rotates much slower
Venus rotates backwards relative to its orbit
Venus is smaller than Earth
quiz.why: The Coriolis effect comes from rotation. Venus turns once in about 243 Earth days, so the effect is weak and its circulation cells are not split up.

order.title: From vapour to rain
order.prompt: Put the steps of making rain in order, first at the bottom.
order.why: Water evaporates, convection lifts the vapour to cooler air, it condenses into a cloud, the drops grow, and they fall as rain, snow or hail.

layers.name: Convection carries the vapour up to cooler air
Vapour condenses into droplets: a cloud

order.title: The carbon dioxide cycle
order.prompt: Follow carbon dioxide around Earth's thermostat, starting at the bottom.
order.why: CO2 dissolves in rain, acid rain wears down rock and rivers carry minerals to the sea, carbonate rock forms, plate tectonics carries it down, it melts and volcanoes outgas the CO2 again.

layers.name: Acid rain wears down rock; rivers carry minerals to the sea
Minerals and CO2 form carbonate rock

order.title: The runaway greenhouse
order.prompt: Put the runaway greenhouse in order, first at the bottom.
order.why: Stronger sunlight warms the planet, more water evaporates, the extra vapour strengthens the greenhouse, the loop repeats until the oceans are gone, then UV splits the vapour and the hydrogen escapes.

layers.name: More water vapour strengthens the greenhouse
Oceans evaporate; carbonate rocks release CO2
UV splits the vapour; hydrogen escapes

order.title: Thicker atmospheres
order.prompt: Order the worlds by how much air they have, least at the bottom.
order.why: The Moon and Mercury have only a thin exosphere; Mars's pressure is under 1% of Earth's; Venus's is about 90 times Earth's.

sort.title: Gas source or gas loss?
sort.prompt: Sort each process by whether it adds gas to an atmosphere or removes it.

items.text: Rusting and other reactions with rock

sort.why: Outgassing, vaporization and surface ejection add gas. Condensation, chemical reactions, thermal escape and solar wind stripping remove it.

sort.title: Reflect more or reflect less?
sort.prompt: Sort each change by its effect on a planet's reflectivity.
sort.why: Ice, aerosols, smog and cleared land reflect more sunlight. Dark roads, cities and open water where ice used to be reflect less.

sort.title: Venus, Earth or Mars?
sort.prompt: Sort each fact into the world it describes.

items.text: Most CO2 locked in carbonate rocks
CO2 freezes at the winter pole
Air stripped after its magnetic field faded

sort.why: Venus: crushing CO2 air, acid clouds, lost water (deuterium), no tilt. Earth: three cells, CO2 in rock, ozone. Mars: seasonal dry ice, huge tilt swings, air stripped by the solar wind.

sort.title: Self-reinforcing or self-regulating?

items.text: Melting sea ice letting dark water absorb heat

sort.why: Self-reinforcing feedback amplifies a change (runaway warming, ice spreading, the screech, melting sea ice). Self-regulating feedback counteracts it (the CO2 cycle, moving the microphone).
